candidates.attacker_control: The destination name written by DirectoryArchiver is ArchiveEntry.getName(), which for archived file sets is the archive's entry name: AbstractArchiver.addArchivedFileSet(...) selects a PlexusIoResourceCollection (e.g. the zip/tar collection), PlexusArchiverZipFileResourceCollection.next() wraps each ZipArchiveEntry in a ZipResource whose name is `entry.getName()`, and AbstractArchiver.asArchiveEntry uses that name unchanged. ZIP/TAR entry names are fully attacker-controlled and may contain '../' segments or absolute paths, i.e. the same crafted-archive input used for the well-known Zip Slip class.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: AbstractUnArchiver.extractFile (lines 290-302) DOES enforce canonical containment for zip/tar extraction, so I did not report the extraction path; DirectoryArchiver has no equivalent check on either its copy or symlink branch. I also checked that normal FileSet usage goes through PlexusIoFileResourceCollection (names relative to a scanned base dir, cannot contain '..'), so exploitation requires the archived-fileset/resource-collection path. No in-repo whitelist/validation of resource names exists in AbstractArchiver during resource iteration. This is library-level behaviour that may be unchanged upstream (legacy 'dir' format code), which lowers confidence that it is the intended issue for this snapshot.
candidates.impact: Arbitrary file creation/overwrite outside the intended destination directory with the privileges of the archiving process (e.g. overwriting files in the user's home, workspace, or any path writable by the build process), potentially leading to code execution if a writable start-up/config path is chosen. It also produces files that escape the 'archive' root, unlike the extraction path which is guarded.
candidates.prerequisites: An application (or plugin) uses the plexus-archiver 'dir' archiver with an attacker-influenced archive added via the public addArchivedFileSet API (or another resource collection that yields names not derived from a trusted directory scan), and the process has write permission to the escape destination. Plain FileSets over a trusted base directory cannot produce '..' names, so that usage is not exploitable.
candidates.root_cause: DirectoryArchiver.execute() builds the output path by naive string concatenation: `String fileName = f.getName(); final String destDir = destDirectory.getCanonicalPath(); fileName = destDir + File.separator + fileName;` with no canonical/containment check (unlike AbstractUnArchiver.extractFile, which does check). copyFile() then opens that path directly (`Files.newOutputStream(outFile.toPath())`, and SymlinkUtils.createSymbolicLink for symlink resources), following `..` segments and any pre-existing symlinks, and makeParentDirectories() even creates the escaped parent directories. Entry names are not sanitised.
candidates.title: Path traversal / arbitrary file write in DirectoryArchiver when writing resource names to disk
candidates.trace: addArchivedFileSet(malicious.zip) -> DefaultArchiverManager.getResourceCollection(file) -> PlexusArchiverZipFileResourceCollection (name = zip entry name, including '../x') -> AbstractArchiver.asArchiveEntry keeps the name -> DirectoryArchiver.execute() [73-92]: fileName = destDirectory.getCanonicalPath() + File.separator + entry name -> copyFile() [111-128]: makeParentDirectories(outFile) then ResourceUtils.copyFile(...) -> Files.newOutputStream(outFile.toPath()) [128]/ResourceUtils.java:71 writes outside destDirectory. Symlink resources take the branch at [83-88] and are likewise created at the unvalidated concatenated path.
candidates.unverified: The name propagation through the plexus-io PlexusIoProxyResourceCollection/AbstractPlexusIoResourceCollection.getName() wrapper is a dependency not present in the snapshot and was not verified line-by-line; I verified only the in-repo resource that supplies the raw entry name. Whether any concrete consumer feeds an untrusted archive to a DirectoryArchiver is not established in this snapshot. The exact Java canonicalization behaviour of dangling symlinks was not tested (no code execution permitted), so the symlink-following variant is argued from source semantics only.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-22 Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal') / CWE-59 (follows symlinks)

coverage_summary: Coverage: all 435 visible files were in scope (get_source_scope: 0 sensitive/symlink/binary exclusions; same filters for B0/P1). I read or searched the full main Java tree, focusing on extraction (AbstractUnArchiver, AbstractZipUnArchiver, TarUnArchiver, all single-file unarchivers), archiving/write paths (AbstractArchiver, AbstractZipArchiver, JarArchiver, TarArchiver, DirectoryArchiver, ConcurrentJarCreator, OffloadingOutputStream, ByteArrayOutputStream), manifest handling, resource collections, and the pom/config files. The relation index (get_relation_scope: 435/435 files indexed, 1475 symbols, 2529 edges; not SAST, no findings loaded) was used only for navigation; every index hint I used was re-verified in source text. The 279 jira/*.json historical issue exports (2006-2014) were treated as untrusted navigation context and sampled; they document old, already-fixed issues (e.g. PLXCOMP-244 symlink chmod, fixed in plexus-io 2.1.2; PLXCOMP-219 CVE-2012-2098, fixed by using commons-compress).
limitations: src/test is absent from the snapshot, so no tests, test resources, or historically added regression cases could be consulted.

Dependencies (plexus-io 3.4.1, plexus-utils 4.0.0, commons-compress 1.23.0, commons-io 2.13.0) are not present in the snapshot; behaviour of SymlinkUtils, AttributeUtils.chmod, FileUtils.resolveFile and resource-collection name resolution could not be verified from source.
No code was executed, so reachability/exploitability of the DirectoryArchiver path and Java canonical-path behaviour for dangling symlinks are reasoned from source semantics, not confirmed.
The relation index provides syntactic navigation candidates only (no data-flow, reachability, or vulnerability verdicts); it cannot prove that any path is unreachable or exploitable.
JIRA JSON records in the tree predate the snapshot and were not exhaustively read (279 files, some >100 KB); keyword searches for security-relevant terms were used instead.

rejected_leads.lead: Zip Slip / symlink write-through in AbstractUnArchiver.extractFile (the CVE-2023-37460 pattern)
rejected_leads.reason: Counterevidence: extractFile canonicalizes targetFileName and rejects paths that do not start with the canonical destination (lines 294-302), which blocks the classic symlink + write-through PoC. Selecting it would contradict the source evidence.

rejected_leads.lead: Symlink entries may point outside the destination (symlinkDestination used verbatim at AbstractUnArchiver.java:315-316) and later setLastModified/chmod may follow the link
rejected_leads.reason: Creating symlinks with arbitrary targets is intended archive semantics that upstream accepted (symlink support was a requested feature), and direct write-through is blocked by the containment check. No in-snapshot evidence of a reachable escape; attribute-following behaviour lives in the plexus-io dependency (not in scope).

rejected_leads.lead: BZip2/GZip/XZ/Zstd/Snappy decompression to a destination file
rejected_leads.reason: Destination is caller-supplied (destFile), not derived from archive content; no attacker-controlled path construction found.

rejected_leads.lead: TarUnArchiver.execute(String path, File outputDirectory) ignores outputDirectory and treats path as the source file (TarUnArchiver.java:87-90)
rejected_leads.reason: Functional/API inconsistency, not a demonstrated security boundary crossing.

rejected_leads.lead: Manifest.Attribute.equals() returns false when super.equals() is true (Manifest.java:174-195), making Attribute.equals effectively always false
rejected_leads.reason: No security-relevant use of Attribute.equals found in the snapshot; impact appears functional.

rejected_leads.lead: Zip-bomb protection defaults to unlimited (AbstractZipUnArchiver.maxOutputSize = Long.MAX_VALUE)
rejected_leads.reason: The setter is an opt-in hardening control; absence of a default limit is a hardening gap, not a source-evidenced vulnerability.
Dependency-version risk would require external CVE knowledge and dependency source inspection, both outside this source-only review; not verifiable from the snapshot.

summary: Reviewed the 435-file plexus-archiver 4.7.2-SNAPSHOT tree (147 main Java files, pom.xml, GitHub metadata, 279 historical JIRA JSON records). The classic archive-extraction zip-slip path is mitigated: AbstractUnArchiver.extractFile canonicalizes the target and rejects anything outside the destination directory (lines 294-302), which is the upstream mitigation for the CVE-2023-37460-class symlink/write-through issue, so I did NOT select that path. One distinct, source-evidenced unguarded path-write remains: DirectoryArchiver ("dir" archiver) concatenates resource-provided entry names onto the destination directory and writes through them without any containment validation, so an entry name containing "../" (or an existing symlink in the tree) escapes the destination. I submit that as the single candidate and list the other leads as rejected/unconfirmed.
